title: Galaxy full of cosmic lighthouses
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3972, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 3972 is a star-studded spiral galaxy in the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear. It lies about 65 million light-years away, so the light reaching us now set out 65 million years ago, around the time the dinosaurs died out.

The galaxy holds two kinds of distance marker. In 2011 astronomers saw a type Ia supernova explode there, though it does not appear in this picture. These explosions all reach the same peak brightness and can be seen across vast distances. NGC 3972 also has many Cepheid variables, pulsating stars whose rhythm of brightening and dimming is closely tied to their true luminosity.

Galaxies with both are especially useful. Comparing the Cepheids with the supernova calibrates how bright type Ia supernovae really are, and that lets astronomers work out distances to far-off galaxies. Accurate distances near and far are needed to pin down how fast the Universe is expanding.
scale: NGC 3972 lies about 65 million light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 3972 in visible and near-infrared light, through filters from 350 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took this image in 2015 for a project aimed at improving the precision of the Hubble constant, the number that describes the expansion rate of the Universe.
